paragraphs: The last chapter shows that the way public business is conducted gives a fairly clear sign of the actual state of morals and the health of the body politic. The more harmony reigns in the assemblies, that is, the closer opinion comes to unanimity, the stronger the general will is. Long debates, dissension and tumult, on the other hand, announce the rise of particular interests and the decline of the State.

This seems less clear when the constitution includes two or more orders, as the patricians and plebeians did at Rome. Quarrels between those two orders often disturbed the comitia, even in the best days of the Republic. But the exception is more apparent than real. Because of a defect built into that body politic, there were, so to speak, two States in one, and what is not true of the two together is true of each separately. Indeed, even in the stormiest times, the plebiscita of the people, when the Senate did not interfere, always passed quietly and by large majorities. Since the citizens had but one interest, the people had but a single will.

At the opposite end of the circle, unanimity returns. This happens when citizens have fallen into servitude and have lost both liberty and will. Then fear and flattery turn votes into acclamation. Deliberation ends, and only worship or cursing is left. That was the vile way the senate expressed its views under the Emperors, sometimes with absurd precautions. Tacitus observes that under Otho the senators, while heaping curses on Vitellius, contrived at the same time to make a deafening noise, so that if he ever became their master, he would not know what each of them had said.

The rules for counting votes and comparing opinions depend on these various considerations. They should be adjusted according to how easy or hard the general will is to discover, and how far the State has declined.

Only one law, by its nature, requires unanimous consent: the social compact. Civil association is the most voluntary of all acts. Since every man is born free and his own master, no one, under any pretext whatever, can make him a subject without his consent. To decide that the son of a slave is born a slave is to decide that he is not born a man.

So if there are opponents when the social compact is made, their opposition does not invalidate the contract. It only keeps them from being included in it. They are foreigners among citizens. Once the State is instituted, residence amounts to consent: to live within its territory is to submit to the Sovereign.[1]

Apart from this original contract, the vote of the majority always binds everyone else. This follows from the contract itself. But people ask how a man can be both free and forced to conform to wills that are not his own. How can opponents be free and yet subject to laws they have not agreed to?

I answer that the question is badly put. The citizen consents to all the laws, including those passed over his opposition, and even those that punish him when he dares to break one. The constant will of all the members of the State is the general will, and through it they are citizens and free.[2] When a law is proposed in the popular assembly, the people is not being asked exactly whether it approves or rejects the proposal, but whether the proposal conforms to the general will, which is their will. Each man, in casting his vote, states his opinion on that point, and the general will is found by counting the votes. So when the opinion contrary to mine prevails, this proves only that I was mistaken, and that what I took to be the general will was not. Had my particular opinion won, I would have achieved the opposite of what I willed, and in that case I would not have been free.
This assumes, of course, that all the qualities of the general will still lie in the majority. When they no longer do, then whichever side a man takes, liberty is no longer possible.

In showing earlier how particular wills take the place of the general will in public deliberation, I pointed out adequately the practical ways of avoiding this abuse, and I will say more about them later. I have also given the principles for fixing the proportion of votes needed to declare that will. One vote of difference destroys equality, and a single opponent destroys unanimity. Between equality and unanimity, though, there are several grades of unequal division, and the proportion can be set at any of them according to the condition and needs of the body politic.

Two general rules can serve to regulate this proportion. First, the graver and more important the questions under discussion, the closer the prevailing opinion should come to unanimity. Second, the more urgent the matter, the smaller the required margin of votes may be allowed to become: when a decision must be made on the spot, a majority of one should suffice. The first rule seems more in harmony with the laws, and the second with practical affairs. In any case, the two together give the best proportions for deciding the majority needed.
